Papertrade advertises zero fees. I went through the numbers on a simple trade and that isn't what I found.

Say you go long Bitcoin at $80,000 with $1,000 of margin at 1000x. Your position is worth $1M, or 12.5 Bitcoin.

Each $1 move in Bitcoin is $12.50 to you. Your $1,000 covers an $80 drop, so your margin runs out at $79,920.

Papertrade liquidates you at about $79,960. That is a $40 drop. At that point you have lost $500 on paper, but they keep the full $1,000.

On the winning side, say Bitcoin goes up $50 to $80,050. Your profit on 12.5 Bitcoin is $625. Papertrade pays you $406, which is 35% less.

Here is what they pay at different move sizes:

A $25 move earns $312 and pays $157. That is a 50% cut.

A $50 move earns $625 and pays $406. That is a 35% cut.

A $100 move earns $1,250 and pays $940. That is a 25% cut.

A $200 move earns $2,500 and pays $2,032. That is a 19% cut.

A $500 move earns $6,250 and pays $5,333. That is a 15% cut.

A $1,000 move earns $12,500 and pays $10,843. That is a 13% cut.

The cut gets smaller as the move gets bigger, but it never goes away.

At 1000x most trades end on small moves, because Bitcoin moves $40 or $50 all the time. Small moves are where the cut is largest.

Putting the two sides together, a $40 drop costs you $1,000 and a $50 rise pays you $406. To break even on those terms you need to be right about 71% of the time.
For comparison, Hyperliquid would charge roughly $900 in taker fees to open and close a $1M position. That fee is stated up front. Your margin also runs all the way to zero before you are liquidated.

On Papertrade the cost comes from the early liquidation and the reduced payouts on wins. Each one shows up in the price you get rather than as a fee. Combined with 1000x leverage, it puts the odds well against the trader.

I shorted the market over the weekend

And then I longed it

And then I hedged

And then I closed a long at the bottom

Then I closed another long at the bottom

I am not a perps trader. I never have been. I've lost money trading perps pretty much my whole crypto career. I don't really have the discipline for it, and I struggle to implement and stick to systems.

I get carried away by narratives, and by emotions. I know all of this.

So the way I do my perps trading is to set aside ~1% of my total portfolio and treat it as gambling money. For some reason, I get a lot more invested (emotionally, intellectually) about how my tiny perps positions are doing and it distracts me from worrying or caring about my longer term spot positions.

So yeah I lost a few thousand dollars doing random shit on perp dexes this weekend, but it prevented me from touching my conviction bags and it entertained my wee little degenerate gambling mind.

Highly recommend segmenting your portfolio and having your long term holds and spot positions (and cash) in one basket, and your gambling positions in another - for leverage, for meme coins, for whatever you want to FOMO in or out of.

Kudos to all the great traders out there who can profit through volatility, but I am more of an investor than a trader, and I know my strengths and weaknesses, and am content with staying in my lane.

🗡️ The Damage Report 🚨 (Oct 18):

Tampered Ledgers drained $91M+ from hundreds of wallets, plus a $141M lawsuit, a data breach and a bunch of wind-downs.

Here's all the damage from the past week in one post:

• Some Ledgers sold through Southeast Asian reseller CryptoBilis had a hidden implant that stole recovery phrases during setup. $91M+ gone. Buy direct from the manufacturer.

• DWF Labs affiliates are suing BitGo for $141M, claiming it sold discounted FF and ESPORTS tokens about two months before their lock-up ended.

• XRP Ledger fixed a 2015 bug that could've minted ~18 trillion XRP at once. Veria Labs' AI agent found it and got the max $250K bounty.

• An attacker used 79thVault's stolen operator key to drain ~$12.5M (16.2K BNB), then sent back 15,000 BNB (~$11M). About as good as a drain gets.

• A breach of Based's card dashboard exposed cardholders' names, passport/NRIC numbers and addresses, tied to their wallets. Expect scammers who already know your name.

• Blur's frontend shuts down November 12. The protocol stays live onchain, and $BLUR keeps the fee switch.

• Relay is retiring its Vaults. Withdraw through the app by December 31, or straight from the contracts after that.

• Edgen, an AI copilot for crypto and stock investors, shut down October 12. Accounts are closed and its X account is suspended.

The XRPL bug is the one I keep thinking about. It sat in the code for ten years and an AI agent found it first… luckily a whitehat.

The "Mythos risk" is real, and I'm not sure every protocol makes it through. The ones that do are gonna come out a lot stronger.

Ultimately, precompiles and EVM are both the wrong place to put most cryptography support into Ethereum. The reason is that precompiles and EVM both operate on data that has to be included into the ethereum chain somehow, which realistically means included in a block as calldata. That space is limited - even with PeerDAS and blocks-in-blobs, there's a practical cap of ~8 MB/s before it starts getting uncomfortable.

Remember: it's not a blockchain. It's a cryptographic world computer. Any data/computation that does not need to be in the "main thread" of data/execution should not be put into the main thread.

Instead, the correct solution is... EIP-8288 maximalism.

If you have any heavy computation that's self-contained, compute it and STARK it client-side (this is quickly getting faster and faster, even on phones), and push the STARK through the EIP-8288 recursive aggregation mechanism. The chain sees the fact that the computation was done and what the result is; it never needs to see the actual data and computation.

This way everyone can use whatever cryptography they want, the Ethereum chain can be lean, and we never need to add more precompiles again.

When we encounter a difficult situation, we like to categorize it.

For example, is this a problem that money can solve? Or, more relevant to the current situation, can we learn something from it and draw useful lessons?

That is what we’ll explore here.

The world’s leading pharmaceutical and biotech analyst is Umer Raffat, who works in New York for Evercore ISI.

As we do every weekend, we listened to his weekly podcast. This time, he opened with the topic of fund performance.

Here are a few things we learned.

First, the chaos in fund performance is not limited to biotech. According to ISI, technology funds are also going through a difficult and chaotic period.

This suggests that the current situation may also be connected to rising interest rates, in addition to the performance of $MRNA, a subject we have discussed extensively before.

Just how chaotic is the situation?

We have already seen junk stocks, led by $MRNA, skyrocket.

At the same time, large pharmaceutical stocks have rallied strongly, benefiting from a flight to safety.

The DRG index has gained approximately 15% over the past year and around 4% since the beginning of October.

To illustrate the chaos, we asked Claude to examine the 13F filings of the 25 largest dedicated healthcare hedge funds and identify their 25 most popular holdings.

We then asked Claude to chart the performance of these stocks this year.

The results show a 32.3% decline over the past month and a half.

Making matters worse, many healthcare funds also held significant short positions in stocks that surged dramatically, including $MRNA, $GRAL, $TWST, $IOVA, $NTRA, and others.

Naturally, this intensified the pain.

So, is the lesson to avoid popular stocks?

Not necessarily.

Even high-quality, attractively valued companies outside the market consensus have experienced aggressive selling.

It appears that investors have been selling quality stocks to chase speculative biotech names and large pharmaceutical companies.

One important lesson is that hedging through the $XBI ETF, which has substantial exposure to speculative biotech stocks, has provided relatively little protection against this particular market rotation.

One way to evaluate the opportunity is through forward valuations.

This distinction could become increasingly important if access to capital becomes more difficult.

The investment conclusion

When we encounter a difficult situation, we like to categorize it.

For example, is this a problem that money can solve? Or, more relevant to the current situation, can we learn something from it and draw useful lessons?

That is what we’ll explore here.

The world’s leading pharmaceutical and biotech analyst is Umer Raffat, who works in New York for Evercore ISI.

As we do every weekend, we listened to his weekly podcast. This time, he opened with the topic of fund performance.

Here are a few things we learned.

First, the chaos in fund performance is not limited to biotech. According to ISI, technology funds are also going through a difficult and chaotic period.

This suggests that the current situation may also be connected to rising interest rates, in addition to the performance of $MRNA, a subject we have discussed extensively before.

Within biotech, ISI reports that market-neutral funds are down approximately 2% this year, while long-biased funds are down by double digits, except for a few fortunate funds that held stocks involved in M&A transactions.

Just how chaotic is the situation?

We have already seen junk stocks, led by $MRNA, skyrocket.

At the same time, large pharmaceutical stocks have rallied strongly, benefiting from a flight to safety.

The DRG index has gained approximately 15% over the past year and around 4% since the beginning of October.

To illustrate the chaos, we asked Claude to examine the 13F filings of the 25 largest dedicated healthcare hedge funds and identify their 25 most popular holdings.

We then asked Claude to chart the performance of these stocks this year.

The results show a 32.3% decline over the past month and a half.

Making matters worse, many healthcare funds also held significant short positions in stocks that surged dramatically, including $MRNA, $GRAL, $TWST, $IOVA, $NTRA, and others.

Naturally, this intensified the pain.

So, is the lesson to avoid popular stocks?

Not necessarily.

Even high-quality, attractively valued companies outside the market consensus have experienced aggressive selling.

It appears that investors have been selling quality stocks to chase speculative biotech names and large pharmaceutical companies.

One important lesson is that hedging through the $XBI ETF, which has substantial exposure to speculative biotech stocks, has provided relatively little protection against this particular market rotation.

What happens next?

One way to evaluate the opportunity is through forward valuations.

Using projected 2031 earnings, certain high-quality biotech companies appear to trade at significant discounts to the broader pharmaceutical industry.

An important distinction is that many of these companies have already successfully completed Phase 3 clinical trials or reached more advanced stages of development.

There are also numerous potential acquisition candidates, including:

$MDGL, $CELC, $COGT, $ABVX, $MLYS, $CGON, $BBIO, $MLTX, $PRAX, $PCVX, $BMRN, $CTMX, $GERN, $IONS, $NBIX, $CYTK, $TVTX, $SNDX, $SVRA.

Another attractive characteristic of some of these companies is that they may not need additional capital to reach profitability.

This distinction could become increasingly important if access to capital becomes more difficult.

Given these conditions, there appears to be little logic in selling high-quality, attractively valued mid-cap biotech companies simply to chase speculative stocks or large pharmaceutical companies trading at historically elevated multiples.

In fact, the current environment may offer an opportunity to establish or increase exposure to high-quality, mid-cap biotech value stocks.

It was important to us to have a unified supply of everything. An alternative would have been to split the supply, half digital, half physical, but then you run the risk of the weights of each becoming uneven. For instance four 1-of-1s get pulled from the digital supply while all four still exist physically, and physical becomes the clear winner for anybody looking for a pack.

We also thought it was important not to become pack insolvent. For instance if nobody wanted to rip a pack and everybody that got a digital pack decided to redeem for a physical, we are now able to process those redemptions and ship everybody their physical packs. If we had split the supply into digital and physical, then we would not be able to fill those redemption requests.
